documents.title: Text of Infection Control and Epidemiology

chunks.content: 1 INTRODUCTION Ankle fractures, common yet significant injuries in orthopaedic practice, have seen a rising trend in incidence, primarily attributed to an aging population and increased sports‐related activities. , This escalation necessitates a deeper exploration into the outcomes and complications associated with ankle fracture fixation, particularly postoperative surgical site infections (SSIs), which remain a major concern in orthopaedic surgeries. SSIs not only pose immediate health risks but also have far‐reaching implications on patient recovery and healthcare systems. , These include severe pain at the infection site, marked swelling and redness, which may rapidly escalate to systemic symptoms like fever, chills and tachycardia. In some cases, these infections can lead to acute septicemia, a life‐threatening condition that requires prompt medical intervention. Early onset of SSIs often necessitates urgent surgical debridement, prolonged antibiotic therapy and, in some cases, may even necessitate the removal of the surgical fixation device to control the infection. The anatomical complexity of the ankle, comprising the distal ends of the tibia and fibula, and the talus, renders it especially susceptible to postoperative complications. The limited soft tissue coverage around the ankle joint further increases the risk of SSIs. Among the various complications associated with ankle fracture fixation, the most common include delayed union or non‐union of the fracture, malalignment and nerve or blood vessel damage. However, postoperative SSIs are not only common but also represent one of the most severe complications due to their potential to significantly worsen patient outcomes. SSIs often led to prolonged hospitalization, additional surgical interventions and, in severe cases, may result in chronic osteomyelitis or amputation. Furthermore, SSIs following ankle fracture fixation can compromise the integrity of the fixation device, thereby jeopardizing the overall success of the surgical procedure. , These infections can manifest in various forms, ranging from superficial incisional SSIs to deep, more severe infections involving the bone and joint structures. Superficial incisional SSIs involve only the skin and subcutaneous tissue and are often characterized by redness, swelling and pain at the incision site. These infections are generally more manageable with local wound care and oral antibiotics. Deep incisional SSIs extend into the deep soft tissues, such as fascial and muscle layers. They can present with discharge, dehiscence or abscess formation and often require more aggressive interventions, including intravenous antibiotics and surgical debridement. The most severe category, organ/space SSIs, involves structures deeper than the fascial/muscle layers, including the joint or bone. These infections, such as osteomyelitis or septic arthritis, are the most challenging to treat, requiring prolonged antimicrobial therapy and potentially multiple surgical interventions. The severity of SSIs can escalate to osteomyelitis or joint sepsis, which are challenging to treat and often require long‐term medical intervention. The consequences of SSIs extend beyond the physical to encompass significant psychological and economic impacts. Patients suffering from SSIs experience prolonged hospital stays, repeated surgeries and often prolonged courses of antibiotic therapy, leading to increased healthcare costs. Moreover, the psychological impact on patients, including anxiety and depression due to prolonged recovery periods, is an area of growing concern. This situation underscores the need for a comprehensive understanding of the risk factors associated with SSIs in ankle fracture fixation to develop targeted prevention and management strategies. The aetiology of SSIs in the context of ankle fractures is multifactorial, encompassing patient‐specific factors, surgical techniques and postoperative care. Patient‐specific risk factors include, but are not limited to, diabetes mellitus, smoking, obesity, peripheral vascular disease and immunocompromised states. These conditions can impair wound healing and increase susceptibility to infection. Surgical factors, such as the duration and complexity of the procedure, use of different fixation devices and the skill level of the surgical team, also significantly influence SSI risk. The postoperative period is critical for infection prevention, with factors like wound care, antibiotic prophylaxis and patient education playing pivotal roles. The purpose of this systematic review and meta‐analysis is to comprehensively evaluate the risk factors associated with the development of SSIs in patients undergoing ankle fracture fixation. By systematically reviewing the existing literature and analysing data from multiple studies, this research aims to identify and quantify the key risk factors. 2 MATERIALS AND METHODS 2.1 Search strategy In conducting this systematic review and meta‐analysis, our methodology was rigorously aligned with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Our meta‐analytical framework was systematically structured around the PICO model, which encompasses: Patient Population (P), referring to individuals subjected to surgical fixation post‐ankle fractures; Intervention (I), which in this context is the ankle fracture surgical fixation procedure itself; Comparison (C), involving a thorough investigation and analysis of a variety of risk factors and their correlation with the incidence of postoperative surgical site infections (SSIs); and Outcome (O), focused on the frequency of SSIs consequent to ankle fracture surgical fixation, alongside an examination of the myriad risk factors that precipitate these

Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Our meta‐analytical framework was systematically structured around the PICO model, which encompasses: Patient Population (P), referring to individuals subjected to surgical fixation post‐ankle fractures; Intervention (I), which in this context is the ankle fracture surgical fixation procedure itself; Comparison (C), involving a thorough investigation and analysis of a variety of risk factors and their correlation with the incidence of postoperative surgical site infections (SSIs); and Outcome (O), focused on the frequency of SSIs consequent to ankle fracture surgical fixation, alongside an examination of the myriad risk factors that precipitate these complications. A comprehensive literature search was executed across four major electronic databases: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library, on September 26, 2023. This search, transcending temporal boundaries, incorporated a meticulously crafted strategy deploying keywords such as “ankle fracture,” “surgical fixation,” “surgical site infection,” “ssi,” “risk factors,” and “postoperative complications.” These terms were meticulously chosen to reflect the extensive spectrum of the PICO framework and to guarantee an exhaustive collation of pertinent studies for our meta‐analysis. No restrictions were imposed based on language. Additionally, the reference lists of relevant articles were meticulously scanned to identify any further potential sources. 2.2 Inclusion criteria and exclusion criteria 2.2.1 Inclusion criteria Study Design: Peer‐reviewed studies including randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, case–control studies and observational studies examining the risk factors for surgical site infections (SSIs) post‐ankle fracture fixation. Participants: Studies involving patients of any age who have undergone surgical fixation for ankle fractures. Outcomes: Studies must report on the incidence of SSIs following ankle fracture fixation, with clear definitions and diagnostic criteria for SSIs. Risk Factors: Studies that specifically investigate risk factors contributing to the development of SSIs post‐ankle fracture fixation. Language: Studies published in any language, provided there is an English abstract available. 2.2.2 Exclusion criteria Non‐Relevant Study Designs: Editorials, letters, conference abstracts, case reports and reviews without original data. Non‐Specific Patient Population: Studies focusing on patients undergoing surgeries other than ankle fracture fixation or studies where the data specific to ankle fracture fixation cannot be isolated. Non‐Specific Outcomes: Studies that do not specifically report on SSIs as an outcome or lack clear diagnostic criteria for SSIs. Incomplete Data: Studies with incomplete data or insufficient detail regarding the methodology or results. Duplicate Publications: Studies that are duplicate publications or sub‐studies of already included articles. 2.3 Data extraction In the meta‐analysis, literature screening and data extraction were conducted independently by two researchers and subsequently cross‐validated to ensure accuracy and consistency. Should any discrepancies arise during this process, the reviewers engaged in a discussion to reach a consensus, resorting to consultation with a third‐party evaluator when necessary. Extracted data encompassed various parameters including the authorship of each study, publication year, the sample size, country of origin, type of study, duration of follow‐up and key risk factors identified. In instances where relevant data were not discernible in the published reports, efforts were made to contact the original study investigators via email to obtain the unpublished data, thereby ensuring a comprehensive dataset for analysis. 2.4 Quality assessment In conducting our meta‐analysis, the methodological quality of each included study was evaluated independently by two reviewers utilizing the Newcastle‐Ottawa Scale (NOS). This scale, recognized for its robustness, assigns a score to each study based on a comprehensive assessment of nine criteria distributed across three key domains: selection, comparability and outcome, thereby facilitating a thorough evaluation of potential biases within the studies. Upon completing this detailed assessment, studies were scored on a scale ranging from 0 to 9. The quality scores were interpreted as follows: studies with scores from 0 to 3 were categorized as low quality, scores between 4 and 6 indicated moderate quality studies and scores from 7 to 9 were indicative of high‐quality research. 2.5 Statistical analyses In our meta‐analysis, the statistical analyses were conducted with a focus on assessing heterogeneity between studies. This assessment was performed using chi‐square statistics, and the degree of heterogeneity was quantified using the I 2 statistic. When the I 2 value was observed to be <50% accompanied by a p ‐value equal to or >0.10, it was inferred that there was no significant heterogeneity among the studies. Under these circumstances, a fixed‐effects model was applied for the computation of the combined effect size. Conversely, significant heterogeneity was indicated when the I 2 value reached or exceeded 50%, or when the corresponding p ‐value was <0.10. In scenarios characterized by such statistical heterogeneity, the random‐effects model was utilized to calculate the aggregated effect size. Sensitivity analysis played a crucial role in our statistical methodology. It was conducted to assess the stability of our findings and to identify any potential sources of heterogeneity. Conversely, significant heterogeneity was indicated when the I 2 value reached or exceeded 50%, or when the corresponding p ‐value was <0.10. In scenarios characterized by such statistical heterogeneity, the random‐effects model was utilized to calculate the aggregated effect size. Sensitivity analysis played a crucial role in our statistical methodology. It was conducted to assess the stability of our findings and to identify any potential sources of heterogeneity. This involved a sequential exclusion of each study from the meta‐analysis, followed by a recalculation of the overall effect size, thereby evaluating the influence of individual studies on the cumulative findings. To investigate the presence of potential publication bias, we analysed the symmetry of the funnel plot. An evenly distributed pattern of data points on both sides of the apex of the funnel plot would suggest a reduced likelihood of results being skewed by publication bias. Furthermore, Egger's linear regression test was employed as a quantitative tool to detect any indications of publication bias. All statistical tests in our analysis were two‐sided. A p ‐value of <0.05 was considered to denote statistical significance. For the purpose of these analyses, Stata version 17 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA) was utilized. 3 RESULTS 3.1 Search results and study selection During the initial phase of our systematic review and meta‐analysis, a thorough search across multiple electronic databases yielded a preliminary collection of 1250 articles deemed potentially relevant. To streamline this pool, a systematic approach was adopted to eliminate duplicate entries, ensuring the representation of each unique study only once. Following this, titles and abstracts of these articles were meticulously screened against a set of predetermined inclusion and exclusion criteria. These criteria were comprehensive, encompassing aspects such as study design, demographic characteristics of the participants, measured clinical outcomes and the overall methodological quality of the studies. This initial screening process led to the selection of 34 articles for a more detailed examination. Each of these articles underwent an in‐depth full‐text review conducted independently by multiple investigators, adhering to an objective and thorough evaluation protocol. During this intensive review phase, 27 articles were excluded due to specific reasons, categorized as follows: review articles ( n = 7), sequentially published studies ( n = 7), studies with inadequate data for meaningful analysis ( n = 7) and clinical trials without control groups ( n = 6). Consequently, after this rigorous selection process, a total of 7 articles were identified as fulfilling all the strict criteria outlined in our research methodology. , , , , , , These articles were thus incorporated into the final meta‐analysis. The process of study selection and the number of articles included at each stage of the review are illustrated in Figure . 3.2 Study characteristics In the meta‐analysis, the characteristics of the included studies were diverse yet systematic. The studies, conducted between 2006 and 2019, were predominantly case–control in design, with a few cohort studies included to enrich the analysis. The sample sizes varied, ranging from as few as 13 participants in the control group to as many as 2543, indicating a broad spectrum of study scales. Geographically, the studies spanned multiple countries, with a notable concentration in China, reflecting the global interest and relevance of the topic. Other countries represented included Japan, Norway, Finland and the United Kingdom, contributing to the international scope of the analysis. The follow‐up periods of these studies also varied, ranging from a year to several years, allowing for a comprehensive understanding of the outcomes over different time frames. This variation in follow‐up periods provided valuable insights into both short‐term and long‐term effects within the respective study scopes (Table ). 3.3 Results of quality assessment The results of this quality assessment revealed that most studies achieved high scores, reflecting their overall methodological robustness. The total scores ranged from 7 to 9 out of a possible 9 points, indicating a generally high quality of the included studies. Each study demonstrated strong representativeness of the exposed cohort and appropriate selection of the non‐exposed cohort. The ascertainment of exposure and the adequacy of follow‐up were also well addressed in most studies. Furthermore, the comparability of cohorts based on design or analysis and the assessment of outcomes were also satisfactorily reported in the majority of the studies. This comprehensive quality assessment underscores the reliability and validity of the findings derived from these studies. Overall, the high‐quality scores across the studies suggest a strong methodological foundation for the meta‐analysis, providing confidence in the robustness and credibility of its conclusions (Table ). 3.4 Impact of diabetes on postoperative surgical site infections In this meta‐analysis, a focused examination was conducted on the relationship between diabetes and the incidence of postoperative SSIs. This comprehensive quality assessment underscores the reliability and validity of the findings derived from these studies. Overall, the high‐quality scores across the studies suggest a strong methodological foundation for the meta‐analysis, providing confidence in the robustness and credibility of its conclusions (Table ). 3.4 Impact of diabetes on postoperative surgical site infections In this meta‐analysis, a focused examination was conducted on the relationship between diabetes and the incidence of postoperative SSIs. Out of the studies analysed, six specifically investigated the impact of diabetes on the occurrence of SSIs. A key component of our analysis involved assessing the heterogeneity across these studies. The heterogeneity analysis revealed no significant variability among the study results, as indicated by an I 2 value of 0.0% and a p ‐value of 0.785. The meta‐analysis results underscored a significant association between diabetes and an increased risk of postoperative infections. The pooled odds ratio (OR) was found to be 1.65, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) ranging from 1.16 to 2.34. This OR reflects a 65% increase in the risk of developing SSIs in diabetic patients compared to non‐diabetic patients (Figure ). 3.5 Influence of smoking on postoperative surgical site infections This segment of the meta‐analysis delved into the impact of smoking on the incidence of postoperative SSIs. The analysis was based on six studies that specifically investigated the relationship between smoking and postoperative SSIs. A critical aspect of this analysis was the assessment of heterogeneity among the included studies. The heterogeneity analysis revealed a considerable variation, as evidenced by an I 2 value of 63.8% and a p ‐value of 0.017. This substantial heterogeneity necessitated the use of a random‐effects model for the meta‐analysis, which is more appropriate in accounting for variability among studies. The meta‐analysis results demonstrated a significant correlation between smoking and an increased risk of developing postoperative infections. The calculated pooled OR for smokers versus non‐smokers was 1.79, with a 95% CI of 1.41–2.27. This OR indicates that smokers have a 79% higher risk of postoperative SSIs compared with non‐smokers (Figure ). 3.6 Association between open fractures and postoperative surgical site infections The heterogeneity analysis yielded an I 2 value of 55.3% and a p ‐value of 0.107. Although this I 2 value suggests moderate heterogeneity, the p ‐value indicates a lack of statistically significant variability among the study results. The meta‐analysis results revealed a substantial increase in the risk of postoperative SSIs associated with open fractures. The pooled OR was 4.87, with a 95% CI ranging from 3.2 to 7.41. This OR indicates that patients with open fractures have an almost fivefold increased risk of developing postoperative SSIs compared with those without open fractures (Figure ). 3.7 Analysis of risk factors for surgical site infections in ankle fracture patients The analysis revealed that age significantly influences the risk of SSIs in patients with ankle fractures. With a fixed‐effects model due to low heterogeneity ( I 2 = 23.4%, p = 0.207), the combined effect showed an OR of 4.65, indicating a marked increase in infection risk with advancing age. This finding, with a 95% CI of 3.06–6.31 and a highly significant p ‐value (<0.001), underscores the necessity for heightened surveillance and tailored postoperative care in older patients. Alcohol consumption was identified as another significant risk factor. The fixed‐effects model analysis, justified by a low heterogeneity ( I 2 = 5%), showed an OR of 1.57. This suggests that patients with a history of alcohol consumption have a 57% higher risk of developing SSIs. The 95% CI ranged from 1.20 to 2.08, and the statistical significance was evident ( p < 0.01). This result emphasizes the importance of preoperative screening and counselling on alcohol consumption. Patients with an American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) score of 3 or higher also exhibited a significantly higher risk of SSIs. The fixed model, chosen due to negligible heterogeneity ( I 2 = 1.8%, p = 0.369), revealed an OR of 2.07. This indicates that patients with a higher ASA score, reflecting poorer general health status, are more than twice as likely to develop SSIs. BMI also appeared as a significant risk factor. With an OR of 0.84 and a 95% CI of 0.37–1.31 ( p < 0.001), the analysis using a fixed model (due to moderate heterogeneity, I 2 = 36%) suggests that higher BMI is associated with an increased risk of SSIs. This finding calls for targeted strategies to manage and monitor patients with higher BMI undergoing ankle fracture surgery. The presence of a contaminated incision significantly raised the risk of SSIs, as evidenced by an OR of 4.63 in a random‐effects model ( I 2 = 51.3%, p = 0.036). This high risk, with a

as a significant risk factor. With an OR of 0.84 and a 95% CI of 0.37–1.31 ( p < 0.001), the analysis using a fixed model (due to moderate heterogeneity, I 2 = 36%) suggests that higher BMI is associated with an increased risk of SSIs. This finding calls for targeted strategies to manage and monitor patients with higher BMI undergoing ankle fracture surgery. The presence of a contaminated incision significantly raised the risk of SSIs, as evidenced by an OR of 4.63 in a random‐effects model ( I 2 = 51.3%, p = 0.036). This high risk, with a 95% CI of 2.94–7.38, indicates the critical need for strict aseptic techniques and infection control measures in surgeries involving contaminated incisions. Fracture dislocation was another identified risk factor, with an OR of 1.74 (95% CI: 1.36–2.20, p < 0.01) in a fixed‐effects model. The lack of heterogeneity ( I 2 = 0%) strengthens the reliability of this finding, suggesting that dislocated fractures are more prone to postoperative infections. Lastly, the presence of heart disease was found to significantly increase the risk of SSIs. The fixed‐effects model analysis, with no heterogeneity ( I 2 = 0%, p = 0.702), showed an OR of 2.97. This denotes those patients with heart disease are almost three times more likely to develop SSIs (95% CI: 1.75–4.98, p < 0.001), highlighting the need for comprehensive cardiovascular assessment and management in these patients (Table ). 3.8 Assessment of publication bias Publication bias was evaluated in this meta‐analysis using funnel plots and Egger's linear regression test. The funnel plots displayed symmetry, suggesting an absence of significant publication bias (Figure ). Additionally, Egger's test results across various variables showed no significant publication bias ( p > 0.05 for all). These findings affirm the robustness and reliability of the meta‐analysis results, indicating that they are not skewed by publication bias. 4 DISCUSSION Ankle fractures are a prevalent injury, especially in the elderly and individuals engaged in physical activities, and represent a significant portion of orthopaedic trauma cases. The management of ankle fractures has evolved substantially, with surgical intervention becoming a cornerstone for ensuring optimal outcomes, particularly in cases involving displacement or instability. , Surgical treatments, ranging from open reduction and internal fixation to more complex reconstructive surgeries, aim to restore the ankle's stability, alignment and functionality. However, the occurrence of SSIs postoperatively presents a major challenge in the management of ankle fractures. SSIs not only delay wound healing and recovery but also increase the risk of complications such as osteomyelitis, chronic pain and even the necessity for additional surgeries. The presence of an SSI can significantly prolong hospital stays, elevate healthcare costs and adversely affect the patient's quality of life. , In severe cases, SSIs can lead to long‐term disability, emphasizing the need for meticulous surgical techniques and postoperative care. Understanding the risk factors and implementing strategies to mitigate SSIs is crucial in the context of ankle fracture management. The negative impact of SSIs on treatment outcomes necessitates a proactive approach, encompassing both preoperative optimization of patient health and rigorous intraoperative infection control measures. This meta‐analysis has identified several critical risk factors for the development of postoperative SSIs in patients, highlighting the complexity of postoperative care. These factors include diabetes, open fractures, smoking, age, alcohol consumption, an ASA score of 3 or higher, higher BMI, the presence of a contaminated incision, fracture dislocation and heart disease. Each of these factors contributes to the heightened risk of SSIs in distinct ways. The strong association of diabetes and open fractures with SSIs underscores the significant challenges in managing patients with these conditions. Diabetes, known for its impact on wound healing due to impaired immune response and reduced blood flow, markedly increases infection risk. Similarly, open fractures, which inherently expose the wound to external contaminants, create an ideal environment for infection. Smoking, age and alcohol consumption were also identified as significant risk factors. Smoking impairs tissue oxygenation and healing, while aging is often associated with diminished physiological reserves and comorbidities, both of which can compromise postoperative recovery. Alcohol consumption can impair immune function and wound healing, further increasing SSI risk. An elevated ASA score indicates more severe systemic disease, which can compromise a patient's ability to recover from surgery and resist infection. Higher BMI has been linked to increased surgical wound complications, possibly due to reduced tissue perfusion and alterations in immune response. Contaminated incisions, by their very nature, carry a high risk of infection, necessitating meticulous surgical technique and postoperative care. The presence of fracture dislocation and heart disease further complicates the postoperative course. Fracture dislocation often results in more extensive surgery, increasing infection risk, while heart disease can limit a patient's physiological capacity to cope with the stress of surgery and infection. The identification of these risk factors provides crucial

Contaminated incisions, by their very nature, carry a high risk of infection, necessitating meticulous surgical technique and postoperative care. The presence of fracture dislocation and heart disease further complicates the postoperative course. Fracture dislocation often results in more extensive surgery, increasing infection risk, while heart disease can limit a patient's physiological capacity to cope with the stress of surgery and infection. The identification of these risk factors provides crucial insights for clinicians. It emphasizes the need for comprehensive preoperative assessments and the development of individualized care plans to mitigate these risks. For high‐risk patients, strategies like stringent glycaemic control, smoking cessation programs, careful wound management and tailored antibiotic prophylaxis should be considered. Moreover, these findings highlight the importance of multidisciplinary approaches involving surgeons, anaesthesiologists, endocrinologists and nursing staff to optimize patient outcomes. Future research should focus on developing and testing targeted interventions to reduce the incidence of SSIs in patients with these identified risk factors. Such studies could significantly contribute to improving surgical outcomes and patient quality of life while reducing healthcare costs associated with SSIs. This study's limitations include considerable heterogeneity in the methodologies and patient demographics of the included research, which might impact the uniformity and applicability of the results. Furthermore, the exclusion of studies published in languages other than English could lead to the omission of pertinent data, potentially affecting the comprehensive nature of the analysis. Additionally, the predominance of observational studies in the dataset restricts the establishment of causality, as these study types are more prone to confounding variables. In the discussion of our findings, it is crucial to acknowledge the implications of the predominance of observational studies in our dataset. Such studies are instrumental for identifying associations but are inherently limited in their ability to establish causal relationships, especially when compared with RCTs. This limitation mainly stems from the absence of randomization in participant selection and potential biases in data collection and analysis. Therefore, while our findings contribute significantly to understanding the risk factors for SSIs post‐ankle fracture fixation, they should be interpreted with caution. These factors collectively necessitate a careful interpretation of the study's conclusions. To overcome these limitations and strengthen future research in this field, we propose several methodological enhancements. Primarily, there is a need for more RCTs, which offer more robust evidence of causality. Advanced statistical methods like propensity score matching and multivariable regression analysis could also enhance the analysis of observational data. Furthermore, longitudinal studies would provide valuable insights into the temporal dynamics of SSIs and their risk factors. Additionally, more detailed reporting of patient demographics, clinical interventions and outcomes in observational studies would facilitate finer adjustments for confounders. Lastly, future meta‐analyses should strive to include a higher proportion of RCTs, thereby yielding a more balanced and comprehensive view of the available evidence. 5 CONCLUSIONS This study identifies diabetes, open fractures, smoking, advanced age, alcohol consumption, ASA score ≥3, high BMI, contaminated incisions, fracture dislocation and heart disease as significant risk factors for postoperative SSIs. Addressing these factors through targeted interventions is crucial for high‐risk patient groups. By implementing specific preventive and management strategies tailored to these risk factors, the incidence of SSIs can be effectively reduced, thereby improving patient outcomes and minimizing the impact of these infections on the healthcare system. chunks.content: 1. Introduction Today, modern housing units must meet new needs and requirements. These depend on various factors, such as the increase in average life expectancy of the population and the increase in people with related functional limitations, new social needs (foreign population, increase in separations and divorces, etc.) [ ], new ways of working (e.g., remote working) and related technological needs, and the development of energy system requirements in response to climate change [ , , ]. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the home, in terms of living space, must be large enough to comfortably accommodate people of different ages, must guarantee sufficient space to fulfill the privacy needs of the occupants, and must be accessible and usable for external users [ ]. The availability of sufficient space in the home, which guarantees the these requirements, is a fundamental aspect in the evaluation of housing quality [ ]. This not only meets a basic human need for shelter, but also contributes to the physical and psychological well-being of the residents [ ]. Although several authors [ , , , ] have dealt with various aspects of the quality of affordable housing in different countries, the discussion on housing standards and space planning is still rather open and leaves room for some considerations [ , , ]. The availability of space in a home affects how and where people prepare and consume food, how they socialise, how they handle household waste and recycling, how they store goods, how much privacy they have for study, work, relaxation or free time, children’s play, to what extent and how they can adapt to new needs (e.g., isolation, disability), etc. [ , ]. A study carried out by the British Commission for Architecture and the Built Environment (CABE) in 2009 [ ] found that 94% of the respondents believed that space in the home was a determining factor in their choice of where to live. Many of the respondents said they do not have enough space to carry out basic activities of their daily lives (spaces for preparing and preserving food, for socialising and entertaining guests, space for study, etc.). Some authors [ ] support the correlation between productivity and the opportunity to work from home. Therefore, an adequate space should meet environmental requirements, mainly related to the needs of person–space relationship based on the activities that are carried out within, but it should also meet psychological needs, hygiene requirements, safety, and full housing usability. The impacts on health of inadequate living space are varied: several are associated with overcrowding, others with accessibility [ ]. Many studies have reported a direct association between crowding and some negative health outcomes [ , ]. These mainly include infectious diseases and mental health problems [ , ]. Such problems lead to a clear inequality in health, as they occur mainly in the low-income population [ , ]. Overcrowding facilitates the spread of airborne infectious diseases (tuberculosis, influenza and related respiratory infectious diseases, meningococcal disease, Covid-19, etc.) and the spread of faecal-orally transmitted diseases [ , ]. The importance of increasing the distance [ ] between people normally recommended in hospital environments has been, and is currently, the main preventive measure, both indoors (homes, offices, shops, etc.) and outdoors, to counteract the spread of Covid-19. In cases of overcrowding, however, it is not only the air transport that plays a role in the spread of the various infections, but also the direct personal contact and the indirect transmission through infected surfaces [ ]. Interpersonal distance and spatial relationships between people and the environment play a fundamental role both in physical health (e.g., transmissible diseases) [ , , ] and in feeling comfortable or uncomfortable in each situation. A review conducted by WHO [ ] also found, via many longitudinal and cross-sectional studies, a significant association between household crowding and mental health problems. These mental health problems include psychological distress, alcohol abuse, depression and unhappiness, social isolation [ , , ]. Reynolds’ 2005 study [ ] carried out on 505 English families showed that more than 70% of those questioned considered overcrowding to be a factor affecting the health of family members; three-quarters of families living in severe overcrowding were also convinced that their children’s health has been affected by living conditions. For 86% of respondents, depression, anxiety, or stress were the result of poor living conditions. Insufficient space does not provide a suitable environment for family life [ ] and can strongly affect family relationships. Space shapes social interaction, determining how much interaction occurs and its results, positive or negative [ ]. Critical issues related above all to the size and layout of housing have emerged strongly even during the lockdown due to the Covid-19 pandemic [ ]; the overlapping of different activities (work, study, socialising, playing)

overcrowding were also convinced that their children’s health has been affected by living conditions. For 86% of respondents, depression, anxiety, or stress were the result of poor living conditions. Insufficient space does not provide a suitable environment for family life [ ] and can strongly affect family relationships. Space shapes social interaction, determining how much interaction occurs and its results, positive or negative [ ]. Critical issues related above all to the size and layout of housing have emerged strongly even during the lockdown due to the Covid-19 pandemic [ ]; the overlapping of different activities (work, study, socialising, playing) in insufficient space can have a heavy impact on family life, creating a difficult dynamic in the relations between inhabitants of the same household [ , ]. Some studies [ , ] attributed a key role to space in determining the quality of family relationships, mainly due to lack of privacy. An adequate space contributes to personal privacy, reducing depression, anxiety, and stress, giving children space to play, and ensuring a good quality of sleep [ ]. Children are more likely to be affected by overcrowding than the adult population, especially if they belong to low-income [ ] families. In the UK, it has been estimated that overcrowding costs the British National Health Service (NHS) over £600 million per year [ ]. Moreover, inadequate housing conditions can be related to symptoms of stress, anxiety, irritability, depression, even social misconduct (violence, vandalism, self-harm) [ ] and alteration of attention capacities at school in children [ , ]. Cassen and Kingdon (2007) [ ] highlight how the home learning environment can play a significant role in performance. Children’s activity is hampered (reduced school performance) by inadequate study space within the home, especially in areas where housing is of inferior quality. It is also accepted that stressful housing conditions can aggravate pre-existing psychiatric pathologies [ , ]. Regarding the health impacts associated with accessibility, failure to meet the occupants’ needs concerning the physical characteristics of the living space can generate impediments to the full use of the premises. In some cases, this can even represent a real source of danger since it can cause domestic accidents. Housing dimensions and functional characteristics are relevant, mainly considering population ageing and disability. In the European Region, the number of people aged 85 years and older is projected to rise from 14 million in 2010 to 19 million by 2020 and to 40 million by 2050 [ ]. As age increases, the percentage of people with disabilities also increases, making the accessibility and usability of homes crucial requirements to improve the ability of these people to live independently, using all indoor and outdoor spaces. This is an important issue, considering that environmental barriers (e.g., stairs and doorsteps) are present in most European homes, making only 27% of homes “easily accessible” by residents [ ], although—under the 2006 UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities—the Member States have the obligation to identify and remove all obstacles to accessibility, including housing [ ]. Domestic accidents are also closely related to the structure and functional layout of the accommodation, as well as the personal characteristics of the inhabitants (e.g., age, habits, etc.). Considering the available evidence, the WHO [ ] strongly recommends housing interventions aimed at preventing domestic accidents, for example, eliminating obstacles and adopting design solutions that take into account the sizing of the premises [ , , ]. For the reasons described above, the reflection on living spaces, over the years, has expanded in the health sector [ , , , , , , ], but also in the technical and economic sectors [ , , , ], due to the need to offer an adequate and sustainable housing supply. Considering the issues described above, this paper, as part of a debate on housing’ dimensional requirements interesting different countries [ , , ], analyses and compares housing condition indicators of some European countries and their housing dimensional standards to evaluate their ability to answer population needs in terms of health and affordability and to define updated indication for Italian regulation. 2. Materials and Methods The study presented in this paper was conducted as part of a research project funded by the Italian Ministry of Health, aimed to update health performance objectives for the construction and/or renovation of buildings in Italy [ ]. research project funded by the Italian Ministry of Health, aimed to update health performance objectives for the construction and/or renovation of buildings in Italy [ ]. In particular, the study focused on the analysis and comparison of Italian housing standards—defined by Health Ministerial Decree dated 5 July 1975—with those of some European countries [ ] to investigate the aspects related to the housing dimensional standards and how these have been dealt with, within the regulations. The interest of the study is to identify performance objectives capable of ensuring a healthy and sustainable home that considers the new needs of the occupants in terms of health, equity and affordability. The study carried out in 2018 and updated between May and August 2020, regarded the research and review of Building codes (BCs) of a sample of West-European countries, following the methodology already applied in previous studies, although with different aims [ , ]. To obtain an updated indicative picture of dimensional requirements in North, Central and South of Western European countries, nine countries were selected, among those most populated ( ) and similar from a socio-economic and development point of view. reports the selected countries, their population and density. Over 365 million people live in these countries, accounting for about 89% of the West European population. They overall represent about half (47.6%) of the resident population of the whole European continent in 2019 [ ]. The BCs were found in the governmental websites of the different member states, as well as in “Energy Efficiency in Buildings” website ( http://www.buildup.eu , accessed on 15 May 2020). The BCs’ analysis, focused on hygienic and sanitary housing requirements in terms dimensional standards and functional characteristics of dwellings, compared the following aspects, if reported: minimum housing size; minimum living space for inhabitant; minimum room size for inhabitant; rooms’ minimum height. To obtain a more reliable evaluation, the BCs were selected and revised from two researchers independently. All the investigated data were reported in data sheets by each researcher and later compared and discussed. In the case of countries with federal structures, their analysis focuses on a single province or region, selected following two major criteria: regulation update and availability of detailed quantitative parameters to compare with the other selected countries. This is the case with Germany and Spain, where the analyses focused on Hessen and Catalonia, respectively. About the United Kingdom, data refer to England and Wales. At the same time, to better understand and justify the differences among the various building regulations, some basic housing indicators of each country were selected and compared. The analysis focused on three main points: housing characteristics, in terms of average housing size, building type (flat, detached, or semi-detached house), housing deprivation (dwellings with poor amenities), to picture the housing supply of each country. distribution of housing tenure status and costs due to different tenure conditions (ownership or tenantship) by country. Housing costs refer to monthly expenditure that is connected to living in a property (e.g., mortgage, taxes, costs of utilities or rental payments for tenants, etc.), to understand housing affordability. Data were selected from Eurostat database of the European Commission [ ] regarding “statistics on housing conditions” and refers to the last data available. 3. Results 3.1. In conclusion, the regulatory documents of Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Spain, and Sweden define their standards mainly based on performance, with some prescriptive requirements. Those of France, Italy and Portugal identify prescriptive standards, accompanied by more recent technical performance standards, specific for each sector. Finally, UK regulation does not indicate parameters but provides some functional indicators. 3.2. Housing Characteristics Comparison in the Examined Countries As observed previously, some social and demographic changes are influencing housing demand: evolving family structures and a growing proportion of elderly people is resulting in an increasing number of homes being required to house a quite similar number of inhabitants. At local level, given the considerable investment that is required, it is often difficult to make rapid changes to the type and the number of houses that are made available to those looking for a new home [ , ]. In the examined countries existing building heritage is generally old, with a large number of constructions built before 1980 (in average, more than 65%) [ ]. This means that several structural problems (e.g., inadequate fixtures causing waste of energy, indoor physical obstacles like stairs, space distributions variation) require relevant investments to be adapted to new need in terms of health and sustainability. The housing deprivation index measures the percentage of the population living in dwellings with poor amenities (e.g., leaking roof; no bath/shower, or no indoor toilet; dwellings that are considered too dark, etc.). Housing deprivation, in 2018, ranges from 5.0% in Italy to 1.3% in the Netherlands. One of the key dimensions in assessing the housing quality is the availability of sufficient space in the home also. The indicator used to evaluate the space availability is the overcrowding rate, as defined by Eurostat, that calculates the percentage of people living in an overcrowded household. A household that does not have at its disposal a minimum number of rooms is considered overcrowded, depending on the household composition [ ]: one room for the household; one room per couple in the household; one room for each single person aged 18 or more; one room per pair of single people of the same gender between 12 and 17 years of age; one room for each single person between 12 and 17 years of age and not included in the previous category; one room per pair of children under 12 years of age. Therefore, for Eurostat, room size does not matter. In its view, the main factor affecting overcrowding is the number of rooms. In 2018, the highest overcrowding rate among the analyzed countries in this study ( ) is recorded in Italy (28.3%), while the United Kingdom (4.8%), and The Netherlands (4.8%) recorded the lowest ones. Discussion The comparative analysis carried out allowed us to identify convergences and divergences in the Building Codes and standards taken into exam. There is a diversified approach among European countries: from a market-oriented approach (e.g., England and Wales), where minimum dimensions are not defined, and a prescriptive approach (e.g., Italy), to a functionality-oriented approach (e.g., the Netherlands). As introduced before, attitudes towards minimum standards of space are specific to places and experiences: they come to reflect fundamental beliefs about the usefulness and purpose of housing. Where housing is seen as an investment good, standards are likely to be seen as a threat; where investment is a weaker driver than the market and the quality of houses is judged on their long-term utility and adaptability, rather restrictive standards are set (e.g., in Italy) [ ]. With respect to the above, the abolition of minimum standards in the England and Wales and the weight given to the functionality of space are strategies dictated by market trends. The market determines what is built: or, more specifically, standards are determined by what people are willing to buy [ ]. The comparative analysis clearly shows that the dimensional standards are very different from each other in terms of both form and rigour and completeness. The Italian legislation dictates stricter requirements than those of other countries, but, at the same time, protects the more vulnerable classes from the point of view of living spaces, defining a larger minimum standard in terms of housing size. These regulations, however, do not always guarantee an adequate level of quality in the home. In fact, 5% of Italian population lives in deprived housing (e.g., dwellings with a leaking roof, or no bath/shower, or no indoor toilet, or dwellings that are considered too dark) and this percentage is the highest among all investigated countries (see ). Furthermore, living spaces themselves, often, do not fully satisfy the needs of users and should be adapted to meet new functional requirements, also for the psychological and physical well-being of the inhabitants. For example, in Japan, the average floor area per person passed from 17.3 m 2 in 1963 to 30.9 m 2 in 1993, which is an impressive improvement [ ]. In a 2005 study [ ], the authors elaborate a comparison of housing size for EU15 by analysing average sizes of new housing, number of rooms and average size of individual rooms. The comparison showed that the average floor area of new homes in the UK, equal to 76 m 2 , was substantially smaller than in any other country. In fact, the average size of new houses in Denmark (137 m 2 ) was almost twice as large as in the UK. In Belgium, Greece, and the Netherlands the average was 50% larger (119 m 2 , 126.4 m 2 , 115.5 m 2 respectively) and almost 50% larger in Germany (109.2 m 2 ) and France (112.8 m 2 ). The average floor area of new homes in Italy (81.5 m 2 ) was the second lowest among EU15 countries, but it can be explained in part by the high costs of houses, especially in metropolitan areas, as well as by the progressively reduced number of household components, due to the demographic drop. Regarding the UK, Evans [ ] reports that compared to other countries, new houses built have a relatively high number of rooms (4.8); the consequence is that the average size of the rooms in new homes, just over 15 m 2 , is smaller than in the other countries. In comparison, new houses in Italy have a limited number of rooms (3.8) with respect to the floor area of the house and the average room size is larger (21.4 m 2 ). The same is for Denmark with a limited number of rooms (3.5) and an average room size of 39.1 m 2 . Portugal and France also impose detailed regulations, although less cautious for the inhabitants than Italy, while in the Netherlands, we find a balanced system between clear performance objectives, health protection and design freedom [ ]. The complete abolition of minimum dimensional standards, for example in England and Wales, has caused considerable controversy. Obviously, freedom from prescriptive minimum size requirements allows the market to meet the needs of a more diverse range of families in the present, but very often, the houses themselves are not adequate for the future because they are unable to adapt to the changing needs of families throughout life. Furthermore, the lack of legal minimum space requirements has led to a reduction in room size; this could contribute to determining serious consequences for the physical and psychological health of the inhabitants. At the same time, some authors [ ] criticize the use of floor space averages as a housing quality measure for several reasons. Firstly, the arrangement of indoor space is potentially more significant as it improves its utility. Secondly, statements about space need to be linked to occupancy levels: relatively large houses can have limited utility if they are overcrowded [ ]. Linked precisely to the size and design of the accommodation is the problem of overcrowding. This not only depends on the number and size of rooms and the number of people sharing the dwelling, but also on their age, relationship, and gender [ , ]. As reported in , in 2019, Italy showed the highest overcrowding rate among the EU states analyzed, equal to 28.3%. This comparison can be confusing because it does not consider that in Italy the minimum room size is defined by the regulations. As shown in , in Italy, the standard defines a minimum room size, based on use, that is much higher than those foreseen in other countries (e.g., a double room of 14 m 2 and a living room of 14 m 2 ). Therefore, considering that Eurostat bases the evaluation of overcrowding on the number of rooms available in the accommodation and not on their size, with the same size, in Italy, the number of rooms available will always be lower than in other countries [ , ]. In Italy, the National Institute of Statistics (ISTAT) measures the crowding of dwellings in terms of the number of family members per square meter of the dwelling (expressed in values per 100 m 2 ) [ ]. We speak of overcrowding if there is a greater number of people present in the home than that resulting from the application of the parameters indicated in Articles 2 and 3 of the Health Ministerial Decree of 05.07.1975 [ ]. These articles refer to dimensional criteria of the rooms, an element that, as mentioned above, does not emerge in the definition of overcrowding by Eurostat and many other international standards, which focus on the number of rooms rather than their size. According to the 15th census of Italian population (2013), on average, in Italian homes the residents have 40.7 m 2 per occupant [ ], a value similar or higher than that observed in other countries [ , ]. It is now widely recognized that housing (both the product itself and the production process) needs significant improvements [ , , ]. Space within housing, living space and the impact it can have on the health of inhabitants is, to date, a key point in the debate on housing. From the technical–architectural point of view, therefore, it is necessary to rethink living spaces by focusing attention on some fundamental characteristics that make for adequate accommodation: flexibility, adaptability and furnishing of the premises and full usability and accessibility of the spaces [ , ]. The small size of the housing, combined with poor construction quality and general standardisation of housing products, is very often a limiting factor for flexibility and adaptability [ ]. As mentioned previously, in recent years, awareness of the importance of housing quality for physical and mental wellbeing has grown considerably [ ] and the recent Covid-19 pandemic has highlighted the absolute need to rethink living spaces by focusing on certain elements necessary to protect the indoor wellbeing [ , ]. In fact, even in the absence of other pollutants, indoor air quality becomes progressively worse the more people there are in a room, especially if the availability of space (volume) per person is scarce. Excluding the already-described risk of easier spread of an infectious disease, stuffy air (mostly due to high concentrations of carbon dioxide) can cause headaches, difficulty in concentration and drowsiness, thus impairing learning performance, without considering the psychological implication of the lack of privacy and individual space [ , , ]. These problems are amplified by the application of sealed fixtures to save energy. Conclusions In conclusion, the appropriate amount of internal space definition for a dwelling is a complex issue. Several factors related to culture, economics, society, affordability, building heritage, influence housing supply and demand, other than health issues. Therefore, we think this topic needs to be assessed with a multidisciplinary and transdisciplinary approach in both research and practice, because of the complexity and wideness of its components. The international trend anticipates the increase of the average housing size, at least in developed countries, both for objective (e.g., sufficient circulation space) and subjective reasons (e.g., claustrophobia problems, infectious diseases prevention, but also private space for working). Today, it is well known that people’s perception of internal space is only partially correlated to its amount, being also related to age and gender. Now, there is limited research on the appropriate size of housing and on its relevance in terms of health, safety, and people’s wellbeing. The needs evolve during time and housing regulations are frequently rigid and unable to be adapted; lower income population groups are those who mainly pay the consequences for this. At the same time, it must be argued that the aspects relating to the size of housing, combined with the adequate sunlight and external view, are of particular importance today, also considering the criticalities overwhelmingly emerged during the recent Covid-19 pandemic. Regarding the Italian regulation, the comparative analysis carried out allowed us to identify the strengths and weaknesses of the MD 5 July 1975, which we highlighted in the previous section, and possible indications for its updating, in line with the provisions of the BCs of the countries studied. The study shows, in fact, the need to integrate some key concepts of the MD 5 July 1975, such as, for example, the one relating to living spaces. It is necessary to introduce a general concept of living spaces to the Italian MD, defining its performance objectives (e.g., room sizing, air volume, etc.) and its minimum performance (usability, accessibility and furnishing), eliminating rigid divisions by rooms. In this view, the MD 5 July 1975 should be updated by defining only the overall living space in proportion to the number of inhabitants. In such spaces furnishing should be guaranteed in such a way as to favor internal accessibility, at least in terms of adaptability according to current regulations. In conclusion, building healthy and safe housing is a complex issue and a multi-sectorial responsibility, achievable only if a contribution is made by all relevant players, since it needs of policy vision, health data, resources, and technical competences. In Italy, the Covid-19 pandemic has placed the country’s profound housing crisis in the spotlight and the large variability between the regions and highlighted the need to address it in a systematic way, considering this important issue in the Country recovery agenda.
